# EU AI Act Compliance for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools: Requirements and Enforcement Status

## Executive Summary
AI hiring tools—covering CV screening, candidate ranking, and worker management—are firmly classified as "high-risk" under Annex III and Recital 57 of the EU AI Act, triggering extensive provider and deployer obligations (high confidence) ([FRA](https://fra.europa.eu/en/project/2023/assessing-high-risk-artificial-intelligence), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/employment-0)). However, the applicable compliance deadline has been legislatively delayed via the "Digital Omnibus" package from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 (high confidence) ([Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-omnibus-vii-deadline-delay-20260)), and no source identifies any concrete enforcement action, fine, or investigation specifically targeting a hiring AI deployer to date.

## Key Findings

### Classification as High-Risk
AI systems used in recruitment and selection—including CV screening, candidate ranking, and worker management—are classified as high-risk under Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (high confidence) ([FRA](https://fra.europa.eu/en/project/2023/assessing-high-risk-artificial-intelligence), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/employment-0)). Recital 57 further specifies that AI used in recruitment, decisions on work-related contractual relationships, task allocation, and monitoring/evaluation of workers falls into this category (medium confidence) ([Recital 57](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/recital-57)). The Act applies extraterritorially, covering non-EU companies whose hiring AI outputs affect individuals within the Union (medium confidence) ([Warden AI](https://www.warden-ai.com/resources/eu-ai-act-hiring-recruitment), [Potomac Law](https://www.potomaclaw.com/news-The-Global-Compliance-Challenge-of-AI-Recruiting)).

### Provider Obligations
Providers of high-risk hiring AI must implement a risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, automatic logging, transparency instructions, human oversight, and cybersecurity measures under Articles 9–15 (low confidence, given weaker source authority) ([ModelOp](https://www.modelop.com/ai-governance/ai-regulations-standards/eu-ai-act)). Before market placement, providers must complete a conformity assessment, issue an EU declaration of conformity, affix CE marking, and register the system in the EU database (high confidence) ([ModelOp](https://www.modelop.com/ai-governance/ai-regulations-standards/eu-ai-act), [Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). For employment/worker-management AI specifically, the conformity route is generally internal-control self-assessment rather than third-party review, unless sectoral product law also applies (low confidence) ([Clifford Chance](https://www.cliffordchance.com/content/dam/cliffordchance/briefings/2024/08/what-does-the-eu-ai-act-mean-for-employers.pdf)).

### Deployer Obligations
Under Article 26, deployers must use systems per provider instructions, assign competent human oversight, monitor operations, retain logs for at least six months, report risks/incidents, and notify workers and their representatives before deployment (high confidence) ([Article 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26)).

### Timeline
The original deadline for Annex III high-risk systems was 2 August 2026, 24 months after entry into force (medium confidence) ([HeyMilo](https://www.heymilo.ai/blog/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know)). However, in June 2026 the Council approved the "Digital Omnibus," pushing this deadline to 2 December 2027 for stand-alone Annex III systems and to 2 August 2028 for Annex I-embedded systems (high confidence) ([Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-omnibus-vii-deadline-delay-20260), [Software Improvement Group](https://www.softwareimprovementgroup.com/blog/eu-ai-act-summary)).

### Penalties
Non-compliance can trigger fines up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover (low confidence given source strength, though widely repeated) ([Goodwin Law](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2024/10/insights-technology-aiml-eu-ai-act-implementation-timeline), [Jaggaer](https://jaggaer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-fines-penalties)).

### Enforcement Structure
Enforcement is shared between the Commission's AI Office, national market surveillance authorities under Article 70, and in some respects the European Data Protection Supervisor (high confidence) ([Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-act-governance-and-enforcement), [Clyde & Co](https://www.clydeco.com/en/insights/2025/05/preparing-for-enforcement-a-guide-to-the-eu-ai-act)). If non-compliance is found (e.g., missing CE marking), authorities must first require corrective action before restricting or withdrawing the system (medium confidence) ([Latham & Watkins](https://www.lw.com/en/admin/upload/SiteAttachments/EU-AI-Act-Navigating-a-Brave-New-World.pdf)). National developments include Italy's Law 132/2025 with criminal deepfake penalties, Spain's AESIA supervisory agency, and Ireland's designation of 15 competent authorities (low confidence, not hiring-specific) ([RAIL](https://responsibleailabs.ai/knowledge-hub/articles/eu-ai-act-august-2026-compliance)).

### Related Legal Frameworks
GDPR Article 22 grants candidates rights against solely automated decisions, operating alongside AI Act obligations (low confidence) ([Kudoswall](https://talent.kudoswall.com/resources/ai-hiring-compliance-guide)). Critics note the AI Act lacks an explicit redress mechanism for hiring discrimination victims, unlike EU equality directives (low confidence) ([CDT](https://cdt.org/insights/discrimination-in-hiring-the-case-for-alignment-of-the-eu-ai-act-with-eu-equality-laws)); the European Parliamentary Research Service also flags this interplay as an open policy question (medium confidence) ([EPRS](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/ATAG/2025/769509/EPRS_ATA(2025)769509_EN.pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources conflict sharply on the binding compliance deadline—2 August 2026, 2 August 2027, or 2 December 2027—reflecting the timing of each source relative to the Digital Omnibus's finalization ([HeyMilo](https://www.heymilo.ai/blog/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know) vs. [CSA](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-omnibus-vii-deadline-delay-20260)). A LinkedIn post claiming hiring-AI penalties "went live" (low confidence) directly contradicts sources confirming the deadline was postponed and obligations had not taken effect ([LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/sohraab-joshi-47a11995_the-eu-ai-act-penalties-went-live-last-activity-7369321030214975490-BCG8) vs. [Software Improvement Group](https://www.softwareimprovementgroup.com/blog/eu-ai-act-summary)). Several claims (conformity assessment route, Italy/Spain enforcement details, GDPR interplay) rest on low-confidence, single-source evidence and should be treated cautiously.

## Knowledge Gaps
No documented enforcement action, fine, or investigation against a specific company for a high-risk hiring AI system exists in current sources. It remains unclear whether the Digital Omnibus delay has completed all EU legislative steps (Parliament approval, Official Journal publication) to be fully binding. The definitive conformity assessment route for employment AI, pending finalized Commission guidelines (issued in draft May 2026), is unresolved, as is the practical interaction between AI Act redress gaps and GDPR/equality law protections.

# EU AI Act vs. US Federal AI Policy: Comparing Requirements for Foundation Model Providers

## Executive Summary
The EU has adopted a binding, legally enforceable regime for general-purpose AI (GPAI) providers under the AI Act, while the US relies on a patchwork of executive orders, voluntary frameworks, and state laws rather than comprehensive federal legislation (medium confidence) ([SIG](https://www.softwareimprovementgroup.com/blog/us-ai-legislation-overview), [Control Risks](https://www.controlrisks.com/our-thinking/insights/ai-visions-in-2026-a-transatlantic-strategic-divide)). Analysts increasingly describe a "transatlantic strategic divide" in 2026, with the EU's rights-based, risk-tiered model diverging from a US approach explicitly framed as "minimally burdensome" and deregulatory (low confidence) ([Control Risks](https://www.controlrisks.com/our-thinking/insights/ai-visions-in-2026-a-transatlantic-strategic-divide)).

## Key Findings

### EU AI Act: Binding Obligations
The AI Act imposes binding, enforceable obligations on GPAI providers under Article 53, including technical documentation of training methodology, publication of a training-data summary, a copyright-compliance policy respecting text-and-data-mining opt-outs, and information-sharing with downstream deployers (medium confidence) ([Orrick](https://ai-law-center.orrick.com/eu-ai-act/general-purpose-ai), [Stanford CRFM](https://crfm.stanford.edu/2024/08/01/eu-ai-act.html)). Models designated as posing "systemic risk" face additional obligations beyond this baseline (medium confidence) ([Orrick](https://ai-law-center.orrick.com/eu-ai-act/general-purpose-ai)). Most disclosure requirements target regulators or downstream providers rather than the public, with the training-data summary being the main public-facing exception (low confidence) ([Stanford CRFM](https://crfm.stanford.edu/2024/08/01/eu-ai-act.html)). Notably, the final adopted text is described as comparatively lighter-touch (transparency-focused) than the EU Parliament's 2023 proposal, which had included database registration and detailed bias/data-governance mandates (low confidence) ([Global Policy Watch](https://www.globalpolicywatch.com/2023/05/eu-parliaments-ai-act-proposals-introduce-new-obligations-for-foundation-models-and-generative-ai), [IBA](https://www.ibanet.org/the-regulation-of-foundation-models-in-the-eu-ai-act)).

### EU Timeline and Enforcement
The AI Act entered into force 1 August 2024 (high confidence) ([Jones Day](https://www.jonesday.com/en/insights/2025/08/eu-ai-act-european-commission-publishes-generalpurpose-ai-code-of-practice)), with Article 5 prohibitions and Article 4 AI-literacy duties applying from 2 February 2025 (medium confidence) ([Prighter](https://prighter.com/resources/eu-ai-act-implementation-timeline)). GPAI obligations became applicable 2 August 2025 (high confidence) ([EC Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/learn-more-about-guidelines-providers-general-purpose-ai-models)), though full Commission enforcement powers only commence 2 August 2026 (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/faq?amp=&combine=&faq_category_id=69)). The Commission published a voluntary GPAI Code of Practice in July 2025 to help demonstrate compliance—explicitly not a "safe harbour"—and pledged good-faith tolerance for incomplete implementation in year one (medium confidence) ([Kennedys Law](https://www.kennedyslaw.com/en/thought-leadership/article/2026/the-eu-ai-act-implementation-timeline-understanding-the-next-deadline-for-compliance), [EC FAQ](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/guidelines-obligations-general-purpose-ai-providers)). Non-compliance can trigger fines up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover (low confidence) ([Lucinity](https://lucinity.com/blog/a-comparison-of-ai-regulations-by-region-the-eu-ai-act-vs-u-s-regulatory-guidance)), and the Act applies extraterritorially to US providers whose systems reach the EU market, akin to GDPR (medium confidence) ([Stackcyber](https://stackcyber.com/posts/ai-eu-act)).

### US Federal Approach
Absent comprehensive legislation, the US relies on executive orders and voluntary frameworks (medium confidence) ([SIG](https://www.softwareimprovementgroup.com/blog/us-ai-legislation-overview)). A late-2025 Trump executive order established a "minimally burdensome" national framework and directed preemption of conflicting state laws (medium confidence) ([ESPAS](https://espas.secure.europarl.europa.eu/orbis/system/files/generated/document/en/Near-term-Future-Transatlantic-Relationship-FINAL.pdf)). On 2 June 2026, EO 14409 introduced cybersecurity mandates and a voluntary "covered frontier model" framework, relying on private-sector cooperation rather than binding mandates, with a national-security emphasis (medium confidence) ([McDermott Will & Emery](https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/new-executive-order-shifts-us-ai-policy-toward-national-security)). America's AI Action Plan (July 2025) outlines 90+ policy actions but functions as directional guidance, not enforceable law (low confidence) ([SIG](https://www.softwareimprovementgroup.com/blog/us-ai-legislation-overview)). The voluntary NIST AI RMF remains a key non-binding reference tool (low confidence) ([Cycore](https://www.cycoresecure.com/blogs/nist-ai-rmf-explained-15-faqs-ai-leader-needs-answered)). States have filled the gap: Colorado's AI Act and California's SB 53/AB 2013 impose their own requirements, though a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force (January 2026) now challenges such state laws under federal preemption efforts (low confidence) ([VerifyWise](https://verifywise.ai/blog/state-of-ai-governance-regulations-united-states-2026), [Wilson Center](https://www.wilsoncenter.org/article/americas-ai-action-plan-after-one-year-what-administration-has-done-and-what-comes-next)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources conflict on the EU's enforcement timeline: obligations apply from August 2025, but Commission enforcement power lags to August 2026 (medium confidence claims, not fully reconciled) ([EC Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/learn-more-about-guidelines-providers-general-purpose-ai-models); [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/faq?amp=&combine=&faq_category_id=69)). It is also unclear which 2023 Parliament proposal elements survived into the final Act text. Several low-confidence claims (below 0.4)—including the "convergence thesis" rejection, the May 2026 omnibus timeline change, and NIST AI 600-1's scope—warrant caution given thin sourcing.

## Knowledge Gaps
Unresolved questions include: the substantive criteria for EO 14409's "covered frontier model" designation versus the EU's "systemic risk" GPAI category; whether Congress has acted on the proposed uniform federal AI framework; how state-federal preemption conflicts will resolve; and whether the US has any binding analogue to the EU's training-data summary or copyright-compliance requirements.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems — internal control (Annex VI) and notified-body assessment (Annex VII) — with the applicable route depending on the Annex III category or, for products already regulated under sectoral legislation, integration into existing procedures ([Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). While the legal framework for designating notified bodies is well defined (Articles 28–35), multiple sources indicate that, as of late 2025/early 2026, the pool of AI Act-specific notified bodies remains very small and no source could confirm a concrete list or count of currently designated bodies (medium/low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Applicable Conformity Assessment Routes
For high-risk AI systems in Annex III point 1 (biometrics), providers must use notified-body assessment under Annex VII when harmonised standards or common specifications are absent or not applied; otherwise internal control (Annex VI) suffices (medium confidence) ([Article 43](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43); [powerquant.dk](https://powerquant.dk/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For Annex III points 2–8, the default route is internal control under Annex VI, performed solely by the provider without a notified body (low confidence) ([dpo-consulting.com](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment); [euaiact.com](https://www.euaiact.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For high-risk AI systems already covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), AI Act requirements are folded into the existing sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies (where applicable) also verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [euaiact.com](https://www.euaiact.com/article/43)).

### Provider Obligations
Providers must maintain a documented quality management system under Article 17 covering compliance strategy, assessment procedures, and change management (medium confidence) ([Article 17](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-17)). Before market release, providers must complete conformity assessment, issue an EU declaration of conformity, and affix CE marking (high confidence) ([Article 47](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-47); [Article 48](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-48)). A new conformity assessment is required for substantial modifications, except for predetermined changes in continuously-learning systems (medium confidence) ([Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Importers must verify before market placement that conformity assessment and technical documentation exist (medium confidence) ([Article 23](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-23)). Article 46 permits derogation from conformity assessment under specified conditions, while Articles 44–45 govern certificates and notified-body reporting obligations (medium confidence) ([Article 60](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-60)).

### Notified Body Designation Framework
Each Member State must designate at least one notifying authority to assess, designate, notify, and monitor conformity assessment bodies (high confidence) ([Article 28](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-28)). Notified bodies must be established under national law with legal personality and meet organisational, quality, resource and cybersecurity requirements (medium confidence) ([Article 31](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-31)). The Commission assigns unique identification numbers and maintains the public NANDO database of designated bodies (high confidence) ([Legalithm](https://www.legalithm.com/en/ai-act-guide/article-35); [artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/35)). Bodies already designated under other legislation (MDR, Machinery Regulation) can reuse existing documentation to expedite AI Act designation (high confidence) ([Article 29](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-29)).

### Current Designation Status (Uncertain)
Multiple lower-confidence sources indicate that as of late 2025/early 2026, very few notified bodies have been fully designated specifically for AI Act assessment, though existing bodies under MDR/Machinery legislation can assess AI components within their existing scope (low confidence) ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act); [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment-what-providers-must-do-zunic-maric-0dfof); [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13907v1)).

### Emerging Simplification Proposal
A proposed "Digital Omnibus on AI" amendment would allow single-application, single-assessment designation across the AI Act and sector-specific legislation, introducing a new Annex XIV to NANDO (medium confidence, not yet adopted) ([Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/WK-3257-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources agree designation is incomplete but disagree on framing (bottleneck vs. routine process); none provide a concrete count or named list of currently designated AI Act notified bodies (low confidence claims from [eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act) and [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.13907v1)). The claim regarding market surveillance authorities acting as notified bodies for law-enforcement use cases is low confidence and unverified in practice ([ai-resources.eu](https://ai-resources.eu/ai-act/testo/capo-03)).

## Knowledge Gaps
No source names specific designated notified bodies or provides a current count via NANDO. The adoption status of the Digital Omnibus proposal remains unclear. It is unknown whether market surveillance authorities have begun operating as notified bodies for sensitive use cases, and no AI Act-specific capacity timeline (analogous to CRA's 2026 target) exists.

# When Do Annex III High-Risk AI System Obligations Apply Under the EU AI Act?

## Executive Summary
The originally adopted EU AI Act set 2 August 2026 as the application date for high-risk AI system obligations, including those in Annex III (high confidence, medium confidence per initial sourcing) ([Snowflake](https://www.snowflake.com/en/artificial-intelligence/ai-governance/eu-ai-act), [GDPR Local](https://gdprlocal.com/ai-risk-classification)). Following the "Digital Omnibus on AI" legislative process through 2026, this deadline has been formally deferred: Annex III (stand-alone high-risk systems) obligations now apply from **2 December 2027**, while Annex I (embedded high-risk systems) obligations apply from **2 August 2028** (high confidence) ([European Parliament press release](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20260611IPR45207/ai-act-ep-approves-simplification-measures-and-nudifier-app-ban), [Council of the EU](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/05/07/artificial-intelligence-council-and-parliament-agree-to-simplify-and-streamline-rules), [EU AI Act Service Desk FAQ](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-ai-act-go-effect-what-its-timeline-implementation)).

## Key Findings

**Original Timeline (Pre-Omnibus)**
Under Regulation 2024/1689 as originally adopted, high-risk AI obligations, including Annex III systems, were scheduled to enter into force on 2 August 2026 (medium confidence) ([Snowflake](https://www.snowflake.com/en/artificial-intelligence/ai-governance/eu-ai-act), [CSA Labs](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20)). The Act itself entered into force on 1 August 2024, twenty days after publication (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/responsibilities-of-european-commission-ai-office)).

**The Digital Omnibus Deferral Process**
The European Commission proposed the Digital Omnibus on AI on 19 November 2025, seeking to defer the high-risk compliance deadline to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I) (medium confidence) ([DLA Piper](https://knowledge.dlapiper.com/dlapiperknowledge/globalemploymentlatestdevelopments/2026/The-Digital-AI-Omnibus-Proposed-deferral-of-high-risk-AI-obligations-under-the-AI-Act)). MEPs supported postponement on 16 March 2026, citing delayed harmonised standards as a threat to orderly implementation (medium confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20260316IPR38219/meps-support-postponement-of-certain-rules-on-artificial-intelligence)). On 7 May 2026, the Council and Parliament reached a provisional trilogue agreement fixing these dates (high confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/05/07/artificial-intelligence-council-and-parliament-agree-to-simplify-and-streamline-rules)). The European Parliament formally approved the simplification measures on 16 June 2026 (high confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20260611IPR45207/ai-act-ep-approves-simplification-measures-and-nudifier-app-ban)), and the Council gave final approval on 29 June 2026 (low confidence, single-source) ([CSA Labs](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-omnibus-vii-deadline-delay-20260)).

**Final Adopted Dates**
The European Commission's official "AI Omnibus enters into force" announcement and the EU AI Act Service Desk FAQ confirm: Annex III obligations apply from **2 December 2027**, and Annex I obligations apply from **2 August 2028** (medium-to-high confidence) ([Digital Strategy EC](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ai-omnibus-enters-force), [AI Act Service Desk FAQ](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-ai-act-go-effect-what-its-timeline-implementation)). One source cites the amending instrument as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entering into force 27 July 2026, amending Article 113 accordingly (low confidence) ([ismscopilot.com](https://www.ismscopilot.com/learn/eu-ai-act-what-applies-from-2-august-2026)).

**Related Obligations**
Watermarking obligations for systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 were separately delayed to 2 December 2026 (medium confidence) ([Lumenova AI](https://www.lumenova.ai/blog/eu-ai-act-delays-july-2026)). Annex III itself lists high-risk categories such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/resource.html?uri=cellar%3Ae0649735-a372-11eb-9585-01aa75ed71a1.0001.02%2FDOC_2&format=PDF), [artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/annex/3)). Providers must complete conformity assessments, CE marking, registration, and incident reporting once obligations apply (medium confidence) ([AO Shearman](https://www.aoshearman.com/en/insights/ao-shearman-on-tech/zooming-in-on-ai-10-eu-ai-act-what-are-the-obligations-for-high-risk-ai-systems)). Deployers must follow provider instructions and assign human oversight (low confidence) ([Regulation AI](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-26)). Non-compliance can trigger fines up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover (low confidence) ([Vigilia](https://aivigilia.com/blog/eu-ai-act-annex-iii-high-risk-ai-systems-list)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Several sources reflect outdated pre-Omnibus assumptions, still citing 2 August 2026 as operative (low confidence) ([Snowflake](https://www.snowflake.com/en/artificial-intelligence/ai-governance/eu-ai-act)), contradicting later EU guidance confirming the 2 December 2027 date. One CSA note explicitly assumed the delay proposal had not been enacted (low confidence) ([CSA Labs](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20)), superseded by later confirmation of final adoption. A GDPR Local source vaguely hedges timing as "late 2026 to early 2027" (low confidence) ([GDPR Local](https://gdprlocal.com/ai-risk-classification)), inconsistent with the fixed December 2027 date.

## Knowledge Gaps
The precise Official Journal citation and publication date of the final Digital Omnibus regulation remain unconfirmed beyond a single low-confidence source. Whether transitional/grandfathering provisions apply to Annex III systems already on the market is unclear. The interaction between the Article 6(3) derogation and the new December 2027 date is unaddressed. How national market surveillance authorities will treat the interim period is also unresolved.
